findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves. They can describe the project after one paragraph.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The top of the page links straight to next steps. That section lists prerequisites, the clone command, `./setup.sh`, and a first command to try (`athena ask "add a changelog"`), so the reader knows exactly what to do.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The homepage shows off a side capability (studying another project), not the main one in the lede (turning a request into a traceable commit). A newcomer never sees an example request, commit, cost record or verdict, so the main promise goes undemonstrated.
findings.source: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project ... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: Almost all of the page is a detailed state-machine description of firstmate, a project the newcomer did not come to learn about. Someone looking for Athena has to scroll past it or decide on their own that it is only a sample.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Why it is built this way", "Claims and sources" (c1–c45)

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to specific lines at a pinned commit. A newcomer can check this traceability for themselves, which backs up the claim of accountability.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."

findings.text: These internal, maintainer-facing items sit in the header and near the end. They mean nothing to a first-time visitor and could confuse them about who the page is for.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision." and "About this page": "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust but does not mention a Rust toolchain among the prerequisites. A newcomer can't tell whether `setup.sh` installs it for them. The page doesn't say, so this is a possible gap, not a confirmed one.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: The page is open about what the study did not check, which builds trust. But it also tells the newcomer that Athena's reading missed whole paths on the first pass, which weakens the showcase a little.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths ... none was run"
